title: How Transformers Work
description: The architecture behind every modern LLM — attention mechanisms, positional encoding, and why scale matters.

data.text: The Transformer is the neural network architecture that powers every modern large language model. Introduced in the landmark 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need', Transformers replaced older recurrent and convolutional networks with a purely attention-based design — and that single change unlocked the scaling that made today's AI possible.

Before Transformers, sequential models like RNNs and LSTMs processed text one word at a time, in order. This made it hard to learn long-range dependencies — by the time the model reached word 500, it had largely forgotten word 1. Transformers solved this by processing all words simultaneously and letting every word 'attend' to every other word.

data.title: Why 'Attention Is All You Need' changed everything
data.text: The 2017 Transformer paper proved that you don't need recurrence or convolutions at all. A model built entirely from self-attention layers could train faster, generalize better, and scale to far more data than anything before it.

Self-attention is the Transformer's secret weapon. For each word in a sentence, the model computes three vectors: a Query (Q), a Key (K), and a Value (V). The Query asks 'what am I looking for?', the Key says 'what I contain', and the Value says 'what I can contribute'. A compatibility score between every pair of words determines how much each word should influence every other word.

data.title: What self-attention computes:
items: Attention scores — how much each word should 'listen' to every other word
Contextual embeddings — each word's representation is updated based on all other words
Parallelism — all words are processed at once, making training much faster

data.text: Instead of running attention once, the Transformer runs it multiple times in parallel — called 'heads'. Each head learns to focus on different relationships: one might track subject-verb agreement, another might track pronoun references, and a third might track semantic similarity. The outputs are then combined, giving the model a richer understanding of language.

Analogy: Multi-head attention is like having several editors read the same paragraph. One checks grammar, one checks flow, one checks facts. Together they produce a better result than any one editor alone.

The original Transformer used two parts: an Encoder that reads and understands the input, and a Decoder that generates the output. The Encoder builds a rich representation of the input text through stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers. The Decoder uses that representation along with its own attention to generate new text token by token.

data.text: Because Transformers process all tokens simultaneously, they have no inherent sense of word order. Positional encoding adds a unique 'address' to each token's embedding so the model knows which word came first, second, third, and so on. The original paper used sine and cosine waves of different frequencies to create smooth, learnable position signals.

data.text: Scaling Laws: Why Bigger Is Better

A key finding from companies like OpenAI and Google DeepMind is that Transformer performance follows predictable scaling laws: as you increase model size (parameters), training data (tokens), and compute (FLOPs), loss decreases in a power-law fashion. This means there is no 'sweet spot' — more consistently equals better, up to practical limits of data and compute.

cards.title: Encoder-Only
cards.description: Bidirectional attention; reads all text at once. Best for understanding tasks.

cards.title: Decoder-Only
cards.description: Causal (left-to-right) attention; generates text one token at a time. Best for generation.

cards.title: Encoder-Decoder
cards.description: Full encoder + decoder; both halves. Best for translation, summarization.
pros: Strong at both read and write

terms.definition: A mechanism where every token in a sequence attends to every other token to compute a weighted representation.
Three vector projections computed from each token. Q asks 'what do I want?', K says 'what am I?', V says 'what I offer'.
Additional information added to token embeddings to indicate their position in the sequence.
Empirical observations that Transformer loss decreases predictably as model size, data, and compute increase.

data.title: Summary
points: Transformers replaced RNNs by processing all tokens in parallel with self-attention
Self-attention lets each word dynamically attend to every other word, capturing long-range dependencies
Multi-head attention learns multiple relationship types simultaneously
Encoder-Decoder is classic; Decoder-only (GPT-style) now dominates generation; Encoder-only (BERT-style) dominates understanding
Positional encoding injects order information since Transformers have no inherent sequence sense
Scaling laws show bigger models + more data + more compute = consistently better performance
data.takeaway: The Transformer's simplicity — pure attention, no recurrence — is exactly what made modern LLM scaling possible.
